narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 52.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is just over 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile of your class, far below the average of roughly the sixth decile among students who were accepted. This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk that you would struggle with the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA came next. At 3.00 it was slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction in the opposite direction, modestly increasing the chance you would pass. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the negative impact of your class rank.

Finally, your family income bracket of upper-middle class worked mildly in your favor compared with the mix of income levels among accepted students, but its influence was the smallest of the three.

Taken together, the model concluded that your academic performance signals a borderline but ultimately elevated risk of failing the bar. To strengthen future applications, you should focus on improving your class rank or GPA in any remaining coursework, consider retaking the LSAT if possible, or look for post-baccalaureate programs that can demonstrate stronger academic readiness.
